adjudication_label: comparative irradiation resistance of RHEA vs Ni alloys
canonical_question: How does the irradiation and helium implantation resistance of nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) compare to standard nickel-based alloys and typical fusion reactor helium production rates?

question_variants.question: How does the resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation compare to standard nickel-based alloys?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The provided text describes the resistance of the W-Ta-Cr-V-Hf alloy to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation (low defect generation, no grain growth) but does not contain any data or comparison to standard nickel-based alloys.
source_evidence_spans: resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation

question_variants.question: How does the '9% He implantation' level compare to typical fusion reactor helium production rates?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The document mentions a 9% He implantation level was achieved but does not provide a comparison to typical fusion reactor helium production rates.

answers.answer: The study notes that resistance was observed even after 9% He implantation, but no comparison to typical fusion reactor rates is provided.
answers.boundary_limitation: No context provided for typical fusion reactor helium production rates.
evidence_spans: Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system.
Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance.

We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth.
